mcqs.question: A fact table is defined at the grain "one row per order." What problem does this create if the business also needs per-product revenue analysis?
options: None — order-level grain supports any analysis as long as you add more dimension tables
The order-level grain can't unambiguously reference multiple products per order, since each fact row can only point to one dimension key per foreign key column
Fact tables can never reference a products dimension
This only matters for snowflake schemas, not star schemas
mcqs.explanation: Grain has to match the finest level of analysis needed — an order with multiple products can't be represented correctly by one order-level row referencing a single product key. Adding more dimension tables doesn't fix a grain mismatch, fact tables reference product dimensions constantly at the right grain, and this issue is independent of star vs snowflake.

mcqs.question: A customer moves from the West region to the East region. With SCD Type 1, what happens to historical sales reports attributing revenue to that customer's original region?
options: They automatically remain correct because Type 1 preserves history
Type 1 prevents the customer's region from ever being updated
They become incorrect — Type 1 overwrites the region value with no history, so old sales now show as East even though they happened while the customer was in West
Type 1 creates a new dimension row so old reports stay accurate
mcqs.explanation: SCD Type 1 overwrites in place with no history, so any report joining historical facts to the current dimension row now sees the new value even for events that happened under the old value — this is exactly the trade-off Type 1 makes for simplicity. Type 2, not Type 1, is what creates a new row to preserve history.

mcqs.question: When does snowflaking a dimension (normalizing it further) typically pay off compared to keeping it as a flat star schema?
options: When a dimension is large, changes often, and update anomalies from denormalization become a real operational cost worth the extra join complexity
Snowflaking is always strictly better and should be the default choice
Never — snowflake schemas are a legacy pattern with no modern use case
Only when using a row-store database instead of a column-store
mcqs.explanation: Snowflaking trades simpler joins for reduced redundancy and cleaner updates — worth it specifically when a large, frequently-changing dimension's update anomalies are a genuine problem. It isn't strictly always better (extra joins have a real cost), isn't obsolete, and the choice isn't tied to row-store vs column-store.

mcqs.question: Why is it better to model a fact table at the order-line-item grain rather than the order grain, even if the current dashboard only needs order totals?
options: Line-item grain uses less storage than order grain
Order grain is technically impossible to implement in a star schema
It has no real benefit — order grain is equally flexible for future analysis
You can always aggregate line items up to order totals in a query, but you can never disaggregate an order-level row back down to individual products once that detail is discarded
mcqs.explanation: Finer grain preserves the ability to answer more detailed questions later via aggregation; coarser grain permanently discards detail that can't be recovered. Line-item grain generally uses more storage, not less, and order grain is entirely implementable in a star schema — it's just less future-proof.

mcqs.question: A dim_customer table for 10 million customers uses SCD Type 2, and the average customer's tracked attributes change twice a year. Roughly how many rows should you expect after 3 years, and why?
options: About 10 million, because SCD Type 2 doesn't affect row count
About 70 million, because each customer accumulates roughly 1 original plus 6 changed versions over 3 years, each as its own row
About 30 million, because only the year matters, not the number of changes
Exactly 10 million times 3, regardless of how many changes occur per customer
mcqs.explanation: SCD Type 2 adds a new row per tracked change, so the row count is roughly customers × (1 + changes per customer over the period) — here 10M × 7 ≈ 70M. This is precisely the storage growth Type 2 trades for preserving history; it clearly does affect row count, and the growth depends on the number of changes, not a flat multiple of years.

mcqs.question: A team ships a warehouse with fact tables aggregated to daily grain because that's all the initial dashboard needs. Six months later, product asks for hour-by-hour analysis. What's the consequence of the original grain choice?
options: The hourly detail was already discarded at ingestion, so answering the new question requires reprocessing historical source data, not just changing a query
No consequence — the daily grain can be disaggregated to hourly on demand
This is only a problem for snowflake schemas
Daily grain automatically supports any finer time granularity without changes
mcqs.explanation: Once data is aggregated to a coarser grain than the source events, the finer detail is gone — there's no query that recovers it, only reprocessing from source data (if it's even still available) can. This is independent of schema shape, and no grain choice automatically supports arbitrary finer granularity later.
